key_clinical_evidence: Proximal weakness improving with brief exercise (post-activation facilitation) is the LEMS signature — opposite of MG.
Anti-VGCC P/Q positive in 85-90% of LEMS; anti-SOX1 strongly indicates SCLC.
Standard CT may miss small recurrent SCLC; PET-CT is the imaging of choice.

specialized_test.impression: Low baseline CMAP amplitudes (deltoid 0.9 mV; reference >3 mV) with 118% CMAP increment on 50 Hz repetitive nerve stimulation, exceeding the >100% threshold. Post-exercise facilitation demonstrated (baseline 0.9 mV increasing to 2.2 mV after brief maximum voluntary contraction). No pathological low-frequency decremental response. Superimposed axonal sensory neuropathy on sensory NCS. The electrophysiological findings indicate a pre-synaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission (low baseline CMAP with high-rate facilitation and post-exercise repair), in contrast to a post-synaptic pattern. Clinical correlation and serological evaluation recommended.
recommended_actions: Correlation with neuromuscular antibody studies recommended.

patient.history_present_illness: A 68-year-old woman with recently completed treatment for limited-stage small cell lung cancer presented with 3 months of progressive proximal leg weakness. She completed 4 cycles of carboplatin/etoposide chemotherapy with concurrent thoracic radiation 6 months ago and achieved a complete radiographic response. At her most recent surveillance visit, she reported difficulty rising from chairs — she now requires using both arm rests to push herself to standing — and difficulty climbing stairs. She initially attributed this to deconditioning after cancer treatment. Her oncologist referred her to rehabilitation, which helped minimally. She has also noted intermittent double vision when driving and reading, occurring in the afternoons but not in the mornings. She mentioned her mouth seems dry most of the time. Over the past 3 months, she has had mild difficulty chewing and her voice becomes nasal in the evenings. She denies sensory symptoms in her hands but has mild numbness in her feet (known carboplatin neuropathy). She denies dysphagia, ptosis in the morning, or respiratory symptoms. Her oncologist ordered a brain MRI and PET-CT which showed no cancer recurrence. She was referred to neurology with the working diagnosis of either carboplatin peripheral neuropathy or paraneoplastic syndrome from SCLC.
